notes.front: What is the AI shared responsibility model?
notes.back: The shared responsibility model extended to AI workloads, dividing security and oversight duties between the provider and the customer.
notes.explanation: AI systems can be steered by the data and instructions people give them, and their outputs may drive important decisions, so they bring duties beyond ordinary cloud services.
notes.example: Like the provider–customer split for a hosted database, but it also covers what staff type into an AI assistant and which company data it may reach.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “AI shared responsibility model”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is prompt injection?
notes.back: An attack that plants instructions in user input or external data to manipulate an AI system’s behaviour or outputs.
notes.explanation: The training unit names it a key AI-specific risk that falls to the customer, not the provider.
notes.example: Like slipping a forged memo into an in-tray that an assistant acts on without question, but the assistant is an AI model reading a document.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “What you typically handle (AI)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In information security, what does confidentiality mean?
notes.back: Keeping sensitive information readable only by the people authorised to see it.
notes.explanation: Encryption is one of its most important controls, but the unit says access controls, secure transmission and clear policies are needed as well.
notes.example: Like a sealed envelope marked for one named person, but enforced by software on a salary spreadsheet.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe defense in depth, “Confidentiality”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In information security, what does integrity mean?
notes.back: Keeping data accurate, complete and unchanged except through authorised processes.
notes.explanation: It gives assurance that what you read back later is exactly what was first stored or sent.
notes.example: Like the tamper-evident seal on a jar of food, but for a signed contract held in a database.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe defense in depth, “Integrity”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In information security, what does availability mean?
notes.back: Making sure data and systems can be reached by authorised users when they need them.
notes.explanation: The unit points out that systems are of no use to an organisation if legitimate users cannot get to them.
notes.example: Like a cash machine that actually works when a customer turns up, but for a company’s online ordering site.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe defense in depth, “Availability”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the Zero Trust principle “verify explicitly” require?
notes.back: Authenticating and authorising every request using all available signals, not a single factor such as a password or network location.
notes.explanation: The more signals that are evaluated, the more confident you can be that the right person is reaching the right resource.
notes.example: Like a card issuer that weighs the card, the shop, the country and your usual habits before approving a payment, but applied to every sign-in.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Zero Trust guiding principles”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the Zero Trust principle “assume breach” mean?
notes.back: Designing security as if an attacker will eventually get through your defences.
notes.explanation: Working on that assumption, you plan to limit what an attacker can reach and to spot a breach quickly.
notes.example: Like a ship built with watertight bulkheads because its designers expect the hull may one day be holed.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Zero Trust guiding principles”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is encryption?
notes.back: Making data unreadable and unusable to unauthorised viewers; reading it again requires decryption with a secret key.
notes.explanation: An attacker who intercepts or reaches encrypted data gains nothing useful without the matching key.
notes.example: Like a diary written in a private cipher, but done by software using mathematical keys.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Describe encryption and hashing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is symmetric encryption?
notes.back: Encryption that uses the same key both to encrypt and to decrypt data.
notes.explanation: Because only one key is involved, it is computationally fast.
notes.example: Like a family home where everyone carries a copy of the one front-door key.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Symmetric encryption”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is asymmetric encryption?
notes.back: Encryption that uses a key pair: a public key that can be shared and a matching private key kept secret.
notes.explanation: The two keys are mathematically related, yet the private key cannot be worked out from the public key.
notes.example: Like a letterbox with a slot anyone can post through, while only the owner holds the key that opens it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Asymmetric encryption”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a digital signature?
notes.back: Data signed with the sender’s private key, which anyone holding the sender’s public key can verify.
notes.explanation: The unit presents digital signatures as something asymmetric encryption makes possible.
notes.example: Like a handwritten signature on a letter, but one that would also show if a single word were changed afterwards.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Digital signatures”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is encryption of data at rest?
notes.back: Encrypting data stored on a physical device, such as a server disk, a database or a cloud storage account.
notes.explanation: Stored data encrypted this way stays unreadable to anyone who lacks the keys to decrypt it.
notes.example: Like locking the filing cabinet itself, not just the office it stands in.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Encryption for data at rest”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is encryption of data in transit?
notes.back: Encrypting data while it moves between locations, such as across the internet, between services or over a private network.
notes.explanation: Data on the move can be intercepted by anyone able to observe the network traffic.
notes.example: Like sending a message in a locked courier pouch rather than on a postcard.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Encryption for data in transit”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is encryption of data in use?
notes.back: Protecting data while it is actively being processed, for example in a computer’s memory or by its processor.
notes.explanation: Data is typically decrypted when loaded into memory for processing, which the unit calls a window of potential exposure.
notes.example: Like reading a confidential file in a sealed, windowless room rather than at a café table.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Encryption for data in use”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is confidential computing?
notes.back: Technologies that create protected execution environments, sometimes called secure enclaves, where data is processed without exposure even to the operating system or hypervisor.
notes.explanation: The unit says this is how encryption of data in use is achieved.
notes.example: Like a sealed booth inside a shared office that even the building manager cannot see into.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Encryption for data in use”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a hardware security module (HSM)?
notes.back: A specialised, tamper-resistant device designed specifically to store and protect cryptographic keys.
notes.explanation: Using dedicated hardware for key storage is one of the key management best practices the unit lists.
notes.example: Like a bank vault, but built for nothing except holding encryption keys.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Key management”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is hashing?
notes.back: Using an algorithm to turn any input into a fixed-length string, called a hash or digest, in a one-way process.
notes.explanation: Because the process is one-way, the original input cannot be recovered from the hash.
notes.example: Like taking a fingerprint: it identifies a person, but you cannot rebuild the person from the print.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Hashing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a rainbow table?
notes.back: A table of precomputed hashes for millions of common passwords, which attackers use to look up matches for stolen hashes.
notes.explanation: It works because hash functions are deterministic: the same password always gives the same hash.
notes.example: Like a reverse phone book, but it maps hashes back to the passwords that produce them.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “How hashing protects passwords”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is salting?
notes.back: Adding a unique, randomly generated value to each password before it is hashed.
notes.explanation: The unit presents it as the defence against precomputed attacks such as rainbow tables.
notes.example: Like a baker adding a different secret spice to each loaf, so two loaves from the same recipe never taste alike.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Salting”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is governance, risk, and compliance (GRC)?
notes.back: The set of practices organisations use to handle regulation, risk and accountability in a structured and integrated way.
notes.explanation: The unit says a structured approach to it brings together policies, operational processes and technologies.
notes.example: Like running a building’s rulebook, hazard log and inspection records as one system instead of three separate folders.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In GRC, what is governance?
notes.back: The system of rules, practices and processes an organisation uses to direct and control its activities.
notes.explanation: Many governance activities arise from external standards, obligations and expectations.
notes.example: Like a sports club’s constitution and committee rules, but for how a company runs its technology.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Governance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In GRC, what is risk management?
notes.back: Identifying, assessing and responding to threats or events that could harm organisational objectives or customer trust.
notes.explanation: Its goal is not to remove all risk but to understand each risk well enough to decide how to address it.
notes.example: Like a head teacher walking round before a school trip, listing hazards and deciding which ones matter most.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Risk”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In GRC, what is compliance?
notes.back: Adherence to the laws, regulations, standards and policies that apply to an organisation.
notes.explanation: Which requirements apply depends on the organisation’s industry, geography and the kinds of data it handles.
notes.example: Like a restaurant meeting food-hygiene rules, but for how a firm protects the records it holds.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is data residency?
notes.back: Regulation of the physical locations where data may be stored, and how and when it may be transferred, processed or accessed internationally.
notes.explanation: These rules can differ significantly from one jurisdiction to another.
notes.example: Like a museum rule that certain manuscripts must never leave the building, applied to where data sits.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is data sovereignty?
notes.back: The concept that data is subject to the laws and regulations of the country or region where it is collected, held or processed.
notes.explanation: Data handled across several jurisdictions can therefore fall under the laws of each of them.
notes.example: Like goods in a port warehouse falling under that port’s customs law, whoever owns them.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is data privacy?
notes.back: The appropriate handling of personal data: any information relating to an identified or identifiable individual.
notes.explanation: Organisations are subject to privacy laws wherever they operate and wherever their customers are located.
notes.example: Like a doctor’s duty over patient notes, extended to a shop’s loyalty-card records.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is HIPAA?
notes.back: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act: United States regulations on protecting and handling health information.
notes.explanation: The unit gives it as one of three familiar compliance frameworks and regulations.
notes.example: Like a hospital’s rule that patient files stay locked away, but written into law and covering every health-data handler it applies to.
introduces: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act

notes.front: What is ISO 27001?
notes.back: An international standard for information security management systems.
notes.explanation: The unit gives it as one of three familiar compliance frameworks and regulations.
notes.example: Like a recognised quality mark for a factory, but for how an organisation runs its information security.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is SOC 2 (Service Organization Control 2)?
notes.back: An auditing standard for service providers that store or process customer data.
notes.explanation: The unit gives it as one of three familiar compliance frameworks and regulations.
notes.example: Like an independent inspection of a storage warehouse, but for a cloud provider looking after customers’ data.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In an on-premises datacentre, which parts of the technology stack does the organisation own?
notes.back: The whole stack; some responsibilities only transfer to Microsoft as you move to the cloud.
notes.explanation: This is the starting point from which the cloud models hand responsibilities over.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Division of responsibility”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: In an on-premises datacenter, you own the whole stack. As you move to the cloud, some responsibilities transfer to Microsoft.

notes.front: Moving from on-premises to IaaS, then PaaS, then SaaS, the cloud provider takes on {{c1::more}} of the underlying security responsibilities.
notes.explanation: The training unit adds that some responsibilities still stay with the customer in every model.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “Shared responsibility in the cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In IaaS, which parts does the cloud provider secure, according to the training unit?
notes.back: The physical datacentre, the network hardware and the host machines.
notes.explanation: The customer keeps everything built on top of those hosts.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “Shared responsibility in the cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Compared with IaaS, what extra does the provider take on in PaaS?
notes.back: The operating system and the runtime environment.
notes.explanation: The customer then looks after application code, its configuration, access controls and data.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “Shared responsibility in the cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In SaaS, what three things does the training unit leave with the customer?
notes.back: Access management, the data, and how tenant-level settings are configured.
notes.explanation: The provider runs the whole application stack and the infrastructure beneath it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “Shared responsibility in the cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which always-retained customer responsibility includes data classification and encryption decisions?
notes.back: Data.
notes.explanation: Azure’s article also puts data protection and compliance with data governance requirements under it.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Responsibilities you always retain”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Data - You're responsible for your data, including data classification, data protection, encryption decisions, and compliance with data governance requirements.

notes.front: Which always-retained customer responsibility covers the laptops, desktops and mobile devices that access your cloud services?
notes.back: Endpoints.
notes.explanation: Azure’s article lists endpoints among the responsibilities you always retain, although its matrix marks client devices as shared under SaaS.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Responsibilities you always retain”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Endpoints - You're responsible for protecting client devices and endpoints that access your cloud services, including mobile devices, laptops, and desktops.

notes.front: Which always-retained customer responsibility covers creating, managing and removing user access?
notes.back: Accounts: managing user accounts.
notes.explanation: It covers the whole life of a user’s access, from creation to removal.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Responsibilities you always retain”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Accounts - You're responsible for managing user accounts, including creating, managing, and removing user access.

notes.front: Which always-retained customer responsibility covers role-based access control, multifactor authentication and conditional access policies?
notes.back: Access management.
notes.explanation: The article says the customer both implements and manages these access controls.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Responsibilities you always retain”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Access management - You're responsible for implementing and managing access controls, including role-based access control (RBAC), multifactor authentication, and conditional access policies.

notes.front: In Azure’s responsibility matrix, who is responsible for configurations and settings under SaaS?
notes.back: The customer, as in every other deployment type.
notes.explanation: The matrix marks this row “Customer” in all four columns: on-premises, IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Responsibility matrix”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Configurations and settings | Customer | Customer | Customer | Customer

notes.front: In Azure’s responsibility matrix, who is responsible for the operating system under PaaS?
notes.back: Microsoft.
notes.explanation: The operating system is the customer’s on-premises and in IaaS, and Microsoft’s in PaaS and SaaS.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Responsibility matrix”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Operating system | Customer | Customer | Microsoft | Microsoft

notes.front: Which defence-in-depth layer includes DDoS protection and perimeter firewalls?
notes.back: Perimeter security.

notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe defense in depth, “Defense-in-depth layers”

notes.back: A data breach.

notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.back: Any two: sign-in location, the device and its compliance, the app being accessed, data classification, anomalies such as unusual sign-in times.

notes.front: In the least-privileged-access principle, what is just-in-time access?
notes.back: Granting access only when it is needed and revoking it afterwards.
notes.explanation: It limits access in time, where just-enough-access limits it in scope.

notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the least-privileged-access principle, what is just-enough-access?
notes.back: Granting only the specific permissions a task needs, rather than broad permissions “just in case”.
notes.explanation: It limits access in scope, where just-in-time access limits it in time.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Zero Trust guiding principles”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two practices the unit links to “assume breach”?
notes.back: Any two: segmenting access, encrypting data end to end, monitoring and analytics to detect breaches quickly.

notes.back: Identities.
notes.explanation: The unit says almost all successful attacks eventually rely on compromising or abusing an identity.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Seven foundational pillars”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Zero Trust pillar monitors health status and compliance and bases access on them?
notes.back: Devices.
notes.explanation: Devices that are out of compliance or show signs of compromise can be blocked or restricted.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Seven foundational pillars”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Zero Trust pillar needs visibility of unsanctioned apps that staff use without approval, and of the permissions apps request?
notes.back: Applications.
notes.explanation: The unit calls applications the way that data is consumed.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Seven foundational pillars”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Zero Trust pillar should be classified, labelled and encrypted so it stays protected outside environments you control?
notes.back: Data.
notes.explanation: The unit says the work in all the other pillars ultimately serves to protect it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Seven foundational pillars”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Zero Trust pillar is continuously assessed for version currency and configuration compliance, with just-in-time access to admin interfaces?
notes.back: Infrastructure.
notes.explanation: Its telemetry lets teams detect attacks and anomalies and respond automatically.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Seven foundational pillars”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Zero Trust pillar calls for micro-segmentation inside network zones, not just at the edge?
notes.back: Networks.
notes.explanation: Segmenting stops a compromise in one part from giving unrestricted access elsewhere.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Seven foundational pillars”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Zero Trust pillar collects signals from the other six and ties them together?
notes.back: Visibility, automation, and orchestration.
notes.explanation: Without it, teams face a flood of separate alerts, which the unit says leads to missed threats and analyst fatigue.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Seven foundational pillars”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the main challenge of symmetric encryption?
notes.back: Key distribution: both parties need the same secret key, and sharing it securely is hard.
notes.explanation: The unit notes that sharing it over a network is especially difficult.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Symmetric encryption”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In asymmetric encryption, data encrypted with the public key can be decrypted only with the {{c1::matching private key}}.
notes.explanation: So anyone can encrypt data for you, but only the private key holder can read it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Asymmetric encryption”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What two things does verifying a digital signature confirm?
notes.back: Authenticity (it came from the expected sender) and integrity (it was not modified after signing).
notes.explanation: Verification uses the sender’s public key against data signed with the private key.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Digital signatures”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: If a cloud storage account holding encrypted data is accessed without authorisation, is the data readable?
notes.back: No, not without the keys needed to decrypt it.
notes.explanation: The unit says the protection remains even when the storage is reached without permission.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Encryption for data at rest”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When you open a website over a secure https connection, which protocol encrypts it?
notes.back: Transport Layer Security.
notes.explanation: It stops third parties reading what passes between browser and server.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Encryption for data in transit”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In what kind of environment does the unit say encrypting data in use is especially important?
notes.back: Multitenant environments, where different customers may share the same physical hardware.
notes.explanation: Secure enclaves keep each customer’s data hidden even from the operating system and hypervisor.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Encryption for data in use”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why should encryption keys be stored separately from the data they protect?
notes.back: If they sit together, an attacker who reaches one automatically has both.
notes.explanation: This is the first key management practice the unit lists.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Key management”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does rotating encryption keys regularly limit?
notes.back: The amount of data exposed if a key is ever compromised.
notes.explanation: Rotation means changing keys periodically.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Key management”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: If the same input is hashed twice with the same algorithm, what happens?
notes.back: The same hash value is produced both times.
notes.explanation: This makes a hash a reliable fingerprint of the data.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Hashing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does a system that stores only password hashes check a sign-in?
notes.back: It hashes the password entered and compares the result with the stored hash.
notes.explanation: The actual password is never stored or transmitted in plain text.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “How hashing protects passwords”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Two users pick the same password. With salting, are their stored hashes the same?
notes.back: No. Each password gets its own salt, so the hashes differ.
notes.explanation: An attacker would need a separate lookup table for every possible salt value.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Salting”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two governance activities in a security context?
notes.back: Any two: data handling policies, identity and access standards, approval for privileged access, control ownership, security strategy direction.
notes.explanation: Governance is the system of rules, practices and processes that directs and controls an organisation’s activities.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Governance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which step of the risk management process discovers risks through interviews, vulnerability assessments, audit findings and monitoring?
notes.back: Identify.
notes.explanation: It is the first step of the process.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Risk”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which step of the risk management process produces a risk score from impact and likelihood?
notes.back: Assess.
notes.explanation: The score helps prioritise which risks need the most attention.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Risk”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which step of the risk management process develops a plan for each significant risk?
notes.back: Respond.
notes.explanation: The plan accepts, mitigates, transfers or avoids the risk.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Risk”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which step of the risk management process tracks risks, measures control effectiveness and updates the assessment?
notes.back: Monitor.
notes.explanation: It is continuous, because the environment keeps changing.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Risk”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When does the unit say an organisation can accept a risk?
notes.back: When its impact is low.
notes.explanation: Accepting is one of four responses, with mitigate, transfer and avoid.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Risk”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which risk response implements controls to reduce the risk?
notes.back: Mitigate.
notes.explanation: The other three responses are accept, transfer and avoid.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Risk”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which risk response uses measures such as insurance?
notes.back: Transfer.
notes.explanation: The other three responses are accept, mitigate and avoid.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Risk”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which risk response changes the process that creates the risk?
notes.back: Avoid.
notes.explanation: The other three responses are accept, mitigate and transfer.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Risk”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Under data residency rules, what must an organisation using cloud services verify?
notes.back: Where the provider physically stores its data, and whether those locations meet the requirements.
notes.explanation: Data residency rules govern physical storage locations.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Data is collected in one country, stored in a second and processed in a third. Whose laws apply?
notes.back: Those of each of the three locations.
notes.explanation: The unit says this is what makes data sovereignty complex across jurisdictions.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does personal data include only obvious details such as names and phone numbers?
notes.back: No. It also covers data that can be indirectly linked to a person, such as location history or browsing data.
notes.explanation: Personal data is any information relating to an identified or identifiable individual.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two things privacy laws require of organisations, according to the unit?
notes.back: Any two: be transparent about data use, obtain consent, give individuals rights over their data, protect personal data.
notes.explanation: The rights include access, correction and deletion.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team moves a web app from virtual machines it runs itself (IaaS) to a PaaS hosting service. Which security task passes to the provider?
notes.back: A: patching the operating system.
notes.choices:
A) Patching the operating system
B) Classifying the data the app stores
C) Deciding which users can reach the app
D) Securing the application’s own code
notes.choicesExplained: C and B stay with the customer in every model. D stays with the customer in PaaS, which leaves application code to the customer.
notes.explanation: In PaaS the provider takes on the operating system and runtime environment.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “Shared responsibility in the cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A firm moves its email to a SaaS service. Which job is still the firm’s?
notes.back: D: deciding who may sign in and with which methods.
notes.choices:
A) Patching the mail server operating system
B) Replacing failed disks in the mail servers
C) Guarding the datacentre building
D) Deciding who may sign in and with which authentication methods
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are infrastructure the SaaS provider manages.
notes.explanation: Identities and access always stay with the customer, whichever service model is used.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “Responsibilities you always retain”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company adopts a SaaS AI assistant. Which duty does the provider typically handle?
notes.back: C: securing the model hosting environment.
notes.choices:
A) Deciding which staff may use the assistant
B) Choosing which company data the assistant can reach
C) Securing the environment that hosts the AI model
D) Training staff on acceptable prompts
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D are customer duties: identity and access, data protection, and user training.
notes.explanation: The provider typically secures the physical infrastructure and AI model hosting.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “What the provider typically handles (AI)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An administrator enables a connector that lets the company chatbot read the sales database. Which AI layer is this?
notes.back: The AI application layer.
notes.explanation: That layer covers which data sources, connectors and plugins the app uses.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “AI shared responsibility model”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A web page contains hidden text telling any AI assistant that reads it to reveal the user’s files. What kind of attack is this?
notes.back: Prompt injection.
notes.explanation: The instructions are embedded in external data to manipulate the AI’s behaviour.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “What you typically handle (AI)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company fits badge readers to its server room door. Which defence-in-depth layer is it strengthening?
notes.back: Physical security.
notes.explanation: That layer controls who can physically reach computing infrastructure.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe defense in depth, “Defense-in-depth layers”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An engineer adds NSG rules so the web tier can talk to the database tier but not to the payroll servers. Which defence-in-depth layer is this?
notes.back: Network security.
notes.explanation: That layer limits which systems can talk to which, reducing damage after one is compromised.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe defense in depth, “Defense-in-depth layers”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An attacker copies a customer list and sells it. Which security goal is targeted?
notes.back: Confidentiality.
notes.explanation: Attackers who steal data are targeting confidentiality.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe defense in depth, “Balancing the CIA triad”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An insider quietly changes bank details on supplier invoices. Which security goal is targeted?
notes.back: Integrity.
notes.explanation: Attackers who modify records are targeting integrity.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe defense in depth, “Balancing the CIA triad”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A botnet floods a ticket-booking site until it stops responding. Which security goal is targeted?
notes.back: Availability.
notes.explanation: Attackers who take systems offline are targeting availability.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe defense in depth, “Balancing the CIA triad”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: You compare the hash of a downloaded installer with the value the publisher lists. Which security property are you checking?
notes.back: C: integrity.
notes.choices:
A) Availability
B) Confidentiality
C) Integrity
D) Non-repudiation
notes.choicesExplained: A concerns access when needed and B concerns who can read data. D is not one of the three properties in the triad.
notes.explanation: The unit gives this very check as an example of an integrity check.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe defense in depth, “Integrity”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Before granting access, a policy checks the user’s location, device compliance and the sensitivity of the file. Which Zero Trust principle is this?
notes.back: Verify explicitly.
notes.explanation: It authenticates and authorises using all available signals.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Zero Trust guiding principles”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An engineer gets database admin rights for two hours to fix a fault, after which they lapse. Which Zero Trust principle is this?
notes.back: Use least privileged access (just-in-time access).
notes.explanation: Access is granted only when needed and removed afterwards.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Zero Trust guiding principles”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company segments its network so a compromised sales laptop cannot reach finance systems. Which Zero Trust principle is this?
notes.back: Assume breach.
notes.explanation: Segmenting access limits what a compromised device can reach.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Zero Trust guiding principles”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A system correlates weak alerts from identity, device and network sources into one high-confidence incident and starts a response playbook. Which pillar is at work?
notes.back: Visibility, automation, and orchestration.
notes.explanation: That pillar aggregates and correlates signals from the other six and automates responses.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Seven foundational pillars”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A thief copies an encrypted backup file but not its key. What can the thief do with the data?
notes.back: A: nothing useful, as it stays unreadable.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing useful: it stays unreadable
B) Read it after renaming the file
C) Read it on a different operating system
D) Read it once it has been hashed
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D do not supply the key, and decryption needs the secret key.
notes.explanation: Encrypted data is useless to an attacker without the corresponding key.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Describe encryption and hashing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team must encrypt terabytes of archived records quickly, on one system that holds the key. Which type of encryption suits this best?
notes.back: Symmetric encryption.
notes.explanation: One key makes it fast and well suited to large volumes, and here no key needs sharing.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Symmetric encryption”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tax adviser wants hundreds of clients to send files only the adviser can open, without agreeing a secret with each client. What should the adviser do?
notes.back: D: publish a public key and keep the private key.
notes.choices:
A) Email each client the same shared secret key
B) Give each client the private key
C) Hash the files before clients send them
D) Publish a public key and keep the private key
notes.choicesExplained: A brings back the key distribution problem. B would let every client decrypt everything. C cannot be reversed to read the files.
notes.explanation: Anyone can encrypt with the public key; only the private key holder can decrypt.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Asymmetric encryption”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Before installing an update, an admin wants proof that it came from the vendor and was not altered. What should be checked?
notes.back: The update’s digital signature, using the vendor’s public key.
notes.explanation: A valid signature confirms both authenticity and integrity.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Digital signatures”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A hospital encrypts the patient database files on its servers’ disks. Which data state is protected?
notes.back: Data at rest.
notes.explanation: Data stored on a physical device, such as a database, is data at rest.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Encryption for data at rest”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Two offices exchange payroll files over the internet through an encrypted tunnel. Which data state is protected?
notes.back: Data in transit.
notes.explanation: Data moving from one location to another is data in transit.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Encryption for data in transit”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A bank analyses customer records in a secure enclave, so even the host’s hypervisor cannot see them. Which data state is protected?
notes.back: Data in use.
notes.explanation: Data being processed in memory is data in use, protected by confidential computing.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Encryption for data in use”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A developer is designing how a web app stores user passwords. What should the database hold?
notes.back: D: a salted hash of each password.
notes.choices:
A) The passwords, encrypted with a key stored beside them
B) The passwords in plain text
C) The passwords, emailed to an administrator
D) A salted hash of each password
notes.choicesExplained: A keeps the key with the data it protects. B exposes every password if the database is stolen. C sends passwords in plain text.
notes.explanation: Storing only hashes means a stolen database gives no passwords, and salting defeats precomputed tables.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “How hashing protects passwords”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An auditor sees that users with the same password have identical hashes in a database. What is missing?
notes.back: Salting: a unique random value added to each password before hashing.
notes.explanation: With salts, identical passwords give different hashes, making rainbow tables ineffective.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Salting”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company creates an approval process that anyone requesting administrator rights must go through. Which part of GRC is this?
notes.back: Governance.
notes.explanation: Approval processes for privileged access are a governance activity.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Governance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A risk register gives a flood risk a score of 12 by multiplying likelihood by impact. Which step of the risk process is this?
notes.back: Assess.
notes.explanation: Assessing weighs impact and likelihood to prioritise risks.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Risk”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A retailer buys a cyber insurance policy to cover the cost of a ransomware attack. Which risk response is this?
notes.back: Transfer.
notes.explanation: Insurance is the unit’s example of transferring a risk.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Risk”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Staff send customer data by personal email, a practice that keeps causing leaks. Management bans it and provides a secure portal instead. Which risk response is this?
notes.back: B: avoid.
notes.choices:
A) Accept
B) Avoid
C) Transfer
D) Monitor
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves the process unchanged. C uses measures such as insurance. D is a process step, not a response.
notes.explanation: Avoiding a risk changes the process that creates it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Risk”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A clinic must prove its patient records meet the national health-data law. Is this governance, risk or compliance?
notes.back: Compliance.
notes.explanation: Compliance is adherence to the laws and regulations that apply to the organisation.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A contract says a council’s records may be stored only in datacentres inside its own country. Which concept is this?
notes.back: Data residency.
notes.explanation: Data residency governs the physical locations where data can be stored.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Records stored in a foreign datacentre can be demanded by that country’s courts. Which concept explains this?
notes.back: Data sovereignty.
notes.explanation: Data is subject to the laws of the country or region where it is held.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A former customer asks an online shop to delete the personal details it holds about her. Which concept gives her this right?
notes.back: Data privacy.
notes.explanation: Privacy laws give individuals rights over their data, including deletion.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Symmetric versus asymmetric encryption: how many keys, and what is each one’s weak spot or strength?
notes.back: Symmetric: one shared key, fast, hard to distribute. Asymmetric: public and private key pair, solves distribution, enables signatures.
notes.explanation: The unit says the freely shareable public key is what lets asymmetric encryption solve the distribution problem.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Types of encryption”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Hashing versus encryption: which uses a key, and which can be reversed?
notes.back: Encryption uses a key and is reversible by decryption. Hashing uses no key and is one-way.
notes.explanation: So encryption suits data you must read again; hashing suits data you only need to verify.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe encryption and hashing, “Hashing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Data residency versus data sovereignty: what does each concern?
notes.back: Residency: where data may be physically stored and moved. Sovereignty: which country’s laws apply to data where it is held.
notes.explanation: Residency is about location rules; sovereignty is about the laws that follow from location.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is being compliant the same as being secure?
notes.back: No. Compliance is the minimum the rules require; security is broader. A compliant firm can still have serious vulnerabilities.
notes.explanation: The unit warns against doing only the minimum required by regulation.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) concepts, “Compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Castle-and-moat versus Zero Trust: what does each assume about a request from inside the corporate network?
notes.back: Castle-and-moat: it is trusted. Zero Trust: nothing is trusted by default; every request is authenticated and authorised.
notes.explanation: The unit says the network perimeter alone is no longer a reliable security boundary.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Describe the Zero Trust model”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which defence-in-depth layer is the innermost, and which Zero Trust pillar ties the other six together?
notes.back: Defence in depth: data is the innermost layer. Zero Trust: visibility, automation, and orchestration ties the other six pillars together.
notes.explanation: The layers are nested barriers; the seventh pillar integrates signals from the other six.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the Zero Trust model, “Seven foundational pillars”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Azure’s article lists data, endpoints, accounts and access management as always retained. How does the training unit group the last two?
notes.back: As one item, identities and access; it also adds configuration choices.
notes.explanation: The unit’s list reads: data, identities and access, endpoints, and configuration choices.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “Responsibilities you always retain”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
